cătăracta (also cătarracta ), ae, f. (cătarractes , ae, m., Plin. and Sol.;
I. v. the foll. ), = ὁ καταρράκτης or καταράκτης.
I. Lit., a waterfall, in gen.; the waterfalls of the Euphrates, Plin. 5, 24, 20, § 85.—Hence,
B. Meton. and κατ̓ ἐξοχήυ,
the celebrated fall of the Nile on the southern borders of Egypt, the Cataract: “novissimo catarracte,” Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 54 .—Acc. catarracten, Plin. 5, 9, 10, § 59; Sol. 32: “pervenit ad cataractam,” Vitr. 8, 2, 6 .—Plur. fem.: “cataractae, nobilis insigni spectaculo locus,” Sen. Q. N. 4, 2, 4 : “praecipites cataractae,” Luc. 10, 317 ; Amm. 22, 15, 9.—
II. In milit. lang., a drawbridge, portcullis, Veg. Mil. 4, 4; Liv. 27, 28, 10 and 11.—
III. A water-sluice, floodgate, Plin. Ep. 10, 61 (69), 4; Rutil. 1, 481 Zumpt.—
IV. A waterbird (that pounces down quickly), Plin. 10, 44, 61, § 126.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
